10465-the-outdoor-girls-of-deepdale-or-c:
Laura Lee Hope published this girls' outdoor story in 1913, sending the Outdoor Girls of Deepdale camping and tramping for fun and health. The girls form a tramping club, face jealousies and taunts, and set out on a tour that tests friendship and nerve. The tone is wholesome, lively, and full of schoolgirl cheer.

A fluttering paper, a leaky boat, a rescue, a wrong road, a barking dog, and a cry of bear fill the tour. A deserted house, a lost girl, and a boy peddler add mystery. Readers get a charming series tale of girls, camping, and outdoor adventure.
14635-ruth-fielding-in-moving-pictures-o:
Alice B. Emerson's Ruth Fielding in Moving Pictures, or Helping the Dormitory Fund, published by Cupples and Leon in New York, belongs to the long Ruth Fielding series for girls. Earlier volumes sent Ruth to Briarwood Hall, Snow Camp, and Lighthouse Point.

Here Ruth helps raise money for her school dormitory through moving pictures, and the schoolgirls face a real fire in the West Dormitory. Ruth dashes out onto the portico and shuts the door behind her, keeping panic from spreading while flames leap inside. The novel mixes school spirit, pluck, and early film excitement.
30119-the-calvinistic-doctrine-of-predes:
Francis Hodgson wrote The Calvinistic Doctrine of Predestination Examined and Refuted, the substance of a series of discourses delivered in St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia, printed in Philadelphia in 1855 by Higgins and Perkinpine. A prefatory letter dated July 13, 1854, bears the names of hearers who asked for publication.

James B. Longacre, Garret Vanzant, John J. Hare, and dozens more write that, having heard Hodgson's recent series on the Divine Decrees, they believe publication would serve the cause of truth. They earnestly desire measures to secure it at an early period. They respectfully solicit Hodgson's concurrence and whatever he can do to further the object. Hodgson answers with the motives that induced him to preach the discourses on the Divine Decrees, opening a published refutation of predestination doctrine from a Philadelphia pulpit.
33367-mentone-cairo-and-corfu:
Constance Fenimore Woolson's Mentone, Cairo, and Corfu, published in 1896, gathers travel sketches of three storied places. Woolson, author of Anne and East Angels, writes of the Riviera town of Mentone, the streets of Cairo's new quarter, and the island of Corfu, with illustrations to guide the eye. Her sketches blend scenery, people, and history in a traveler's warm, observant voice.

The book suits armchair travelers and readers of American letters abroad, as Woolson notes both beauty and the small frictions of travel. Its chapters move from Mediterranean light to Egyptian bustle and Ionian calm. For those who love nineteenth-century travel writing, it is a pleasant, well-observed tour of three lands in one volume.
76548-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, number one, was published every Saturday from March 31, 1832. Its first article, Reading for All, quotes a book on the poor from 1673 that proposed suppressing most stage-coaches and caravans, especially those within forty, fifty, or sixty miles of London. The magazine notes that the evil of stage-coaches is hard to perceive at the present day.

The Penny Magazine was the first great cheap weekly for working readers, giving woodcuts, science, history, and travel at a penny, without politics or religion. It reached hundreds of thousands. This first number shows the venture at its hopeful start.
76590-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, number two, was published on Saturday, April 7, 1832. Its lead article, with a restored view as picture, treats Pompeii. The piece draws on the Library of Entertaining Knowledge volume and on a correspondent who visited the spot. It marvels that the city lay undiscovered so long. Ruins stood within two feet of the surface in places, and country people dug up worked marble for years.

A canal cut in the fifteenth century from the river Sarno runs dark under the temple of Isis, crossing the buried city end to end. Walkers round the walls see the volcanic matter heaped as if hands had piled it there. The shower of ash and pumice buried Pompeii and only Pompeii, leaving the plain toward Naples near its old level. Herculaneum, buried by lava, offers the contrast.
76670-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
A society for spreading useful knowledge among working men published a penny weekly in London. Number three bears the date Saturday, April 14, 1832. Its first piece tells the tale of Somerset House, built in 1549 by the Protector Somerset on the ruins of a church, an inn of court, and men's homes. No pay was made to those turned out.

Somerset died on the scaffold in 1552 and did not long enjoy his palace. Queens kept court there after him, in pomp and strife. The new house was begun in 1774 from the plans of William Chambers. Stamp, victualling, audit, and navy offices fill it, with rooms for the learned societies. A second piece takes up emigration to the North American colonies. Cheap print was the point of the whole: sound knowledge at a penny a week.
76734-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, number nine, was published every Saturday, here for May twenty sixth, eighteen thirty two. A lead article treats butter, with a woodcut of a Yorkshire cow. Beckmann studied the use of butter in antiquity with great learning, the article says. His key finding heads the page. Greeks and Romans did not use butter in cooking.

No ancient medical writer names butter as food, though they speak of it for other uses, the article notes. Apicius, the Roman writer on cookery, never names it. Writers on farming give full word on milk, cheese, and oil but none on butter. The ancients had good oil, the piece holds. Butter is still little used in Italy, Spain, Portugal, and southern France. In England and Holland butter is reckoned the best. Working readers got cheap, sound knowledge weekly.
76752-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge came out every Saturday. This number, dated May 12, 1832, opens with the cathedral of St Paul's. A south view of old St Paul's heads the article. The hill, the writer says, seems marked out from ancient times for public purposes. Some antiquaries claimed a Roman temple of Diana stood there. Sir Christopher Wren, digging the foundations, found no support for that claim.

Wren's workmen did find Roman funeral vases and other burial gear deep below. Rows of ancient British skeletons lay next, and Saxons in stone coffins above them. The first recorded church on the site rose about the year 610, built by Ethelbert, king of Kent. Erkenwald, the bishop who died in 681, improved it. Burned down in 961, it was rebuilt the same year.
76753-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, issue number eleven, was published every Saturday; this number is dated 2 June 1832. Its lead piece treats the crocodile. The magazine had already printed an account of killing the hippopotamus from Doctor Rüppell's Travels, and it now adds his account of how the crocodile is caught in Dongola.

The best season for the hunt is winter, when the beast sleeps on sandbanks in the sun. The hunter digs a hole in the sand on the lee side and hides. When the crocodile sleeps, he darts his harpoon with all his might. The iron must sink four inches deep for the barb to hold. The wounded beast flies to the water while the hunter runs for his canoe. A float on the harpoon cord shows where the crocodile has gone.
76818-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, number thirteen, was published on Saturday, June 16, 1832. The weekly sold for a penny and carried instruction to working readers. Its lead article describes the Natural Bridge of Virginia, with a picture of the rock arch over its stream. Virginia, the article says, is intersected by the Blue Ridge, which divides the state into two parts. The Shenandoah valley west of the ridge is its subject.

Harper's Ferry, where the Shenandoah joins the Potomac through a gap in the mountains, is described first. The Natural Bridge itself, in Rockbridge County, is then reached from a small and uncomfortable tavern. The road runs right over the bridge, and travelers in closed carriages have crossed without knowing it. This number is one weekly issue of the famous penny series.
76874-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of June 30, 1832 was a Saturday number of a cheap weekly for working readers. The Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge published it in London. Each number cost a penny and carried short improving articles with woodcut pictures. This number leads with the cave of Elephanta in India.

Elephanta is an island in Bombay harbour, seven miles from Bombay castle. The natives call it Goripura, or Mountain City. A colossal stone elephant gave the island its familiar name. The statue measured 13 feet 2 inches from forehead to tail. Inside the hill stands a great temple hewn from living rock. Its massy columns seem to hold up the mountain itself. Gigantic stone figures line the dim walls. The article lingers on the mystery of who carved it, and when.
76897-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine was a cheap weekly paper put out by the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. It came out every Saturday and aimed to teach working readers about the wider world. The issue shown here is dated July 7, 1832. Its lead piece, sent in by a correspondent, describes the Cape buffalo of South Africa.

That account draws on what hunters and settlers told the writer during his stay at the Cape. It portrays the buffalo as fierce and sly, an animal that hides in thick cover and charges without warning. It also tells how the beast may trample and gore a fallen man again and again. The piece mixes close report with the tall tales of the hunt.
76910-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine was the cheap weekly paper of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, sold for a penny to bring sound reading to working people. The issue of Saturday, July 14, 1832, the eighteenth number, leads with a long account of the Colosseum at Rome. The article tells how the great amphitheatre was begun by Vespasian and finished by Titus, and describes the beast fights and shows that filled it under the emperors.

The magazine mixed history, natural knowledge, and useful facts in plain prose, with woodcut pictures to draw the eye. Its Colosseum piece dwells on the size of the ruin, nearly six acres, and on what later ages stole from it for their own temples and palaces. Numbers like this one carried the society's project into cottages and workshops across Britain.
77006-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine for August 4, 1832, is number twenty-two of a weekly issued every Saturday. The Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge published it. Its first article treats Warwick Castle, with a picture of the castle from the Avon. The castle rises from solid rock above the river.

The writer calls it one of the most interesting monuments of feudal grandeur in the kingdom. Caesar's Tower and the island view get a second picture. A road cut through rock hides the castle until it bursts on the visitor's eye. Two towers of high antiquity still stand entire. The magazine brought such sights, cheaply printed, to readers who could never travel to see them.
77007-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, number twenty three, was published every Saturday, here for August eleventh, eighteen thirty two. A lead article treats the olive, with a woodcut of the olive tree. Something mild and graceful marks the olive look, the article says. Its leaves resemble the willow, only softer and more delicate. The wild olive grows in Syria, Greece, and Africa.

The flowers come in little spikes, pale yellow at first, then white within with a yellow centre. The cultivated olive grows freely round the Levant where frosty winds spare it. The plain of Athens, seen from Mount Hymettus, appears covered with olive trees, the piece notes. Tuscany, southern France, and Spain first grew the olive in Europe. Tuscans first exported olive oil largely, hence the name Florence oil. Working readers got cheap botany and trade lore weekly.
77008-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine came out every Saturday from the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. This issue, number 24, is dated August 18, 1832. The society aimed to put sound, cheap reading into the hands of working people, at a penny a week.

The lead piece describes Constantinople. It sets the city on its point between Europe and Asia, with the Bosphorus running like a stately river to the Sea of Marmora. The Golden Horn, the piece says, may be the finest harbor in the world. The writer traces the site from Byzantium, founded long before Rome's empire, to Constantine's new capital of about the year 330. A view of the city heads the article.
77139-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine was a cheap weekly from the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. The copy here is the issue of September 1, 1832, sold each Saturday. Its first tale, with a view, tells of Westminster Bridge in London. A note says that a century back, no bridge but one spanned the Thames there.

The tale tells how a law of 1735 let a second bridge be built at last. Boat men and the City fought the plan, since they gained from the old ways. Work began in 1738, with piles driven as a vast crowd watched. Stone piers, some blocks of four or five tons, rose in dams built in the stream. Cheap print of this sort brought facts on works and craft to poor readers.
77140-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine was a cheap weekly from the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. Number twenty-nine came out on Saturday, September 15, 1832. Its lead article describes the Warwick Vase, a famous work of ancient art then standing in the grounds of Warwick Castle. A picture shows the wide vase with its sculpted heads.

The vase, the article says, was dug from the ruins of the Emperor Adrian's villa at Tivoli. Sir William Hamilton sent it to England in 1774. It is made of white marble, nearly round, with a deep rim. Vine stems form its two handles, and antique heads stand out in high relief. The magazine used such pieces to teach art and history to working readers for a penny.
77141-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine spread useful knowledge each Saturday for the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. The issue dated September 29, 1832, leads with the British Museum and its famed vase. That vase, called Portland or Barberini, stands in a small room by the stairs. Fine pictures show its blue glass ground and white raised forms.

The piece gives the size of the vase and guesses how its two parts were joined by heat. No firm tale for its scene has yet been found, the writer grants. Grace and pathos in the forms still move all who see them. Cheap print thus brought great art within reach of poor readers.
77196-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine came out each Saturday from the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, a group set on cheap learning for all. This number, dated October 13, 1832, sold for one penny. A woodcut of the Temple of the Sibyl heads the lead piece.

The lead piece tours Tivoli, a hill town near Rome famed for its falls and old temples. Groves, ruins, and villas line the road Horace once walked. The town holds near ten thousand souls, poor but hale in the hill air. Such pieces mixed travel, art, and fact in short, clear prose. The magazine brought the world to working readers who had few books and less cash.
77197-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, number 35, came out on Saturday, October 20, 1832. The lead article, Catching Turtles, is pictured with a plate of the work on the coast of Cuba. It begins at the docks, where a cargo of turtles lands on its back, helpless-looking, the green fat in fine order for the table.

The article then turns naturalist. Turtle and tortoise belong to one group of reptiles; the turtle is the water kind, found on land only now and then. Two kinds fill the plate, the Green Tortoise, chiefly used for food, and the Loggerhead. The green sort gathers in great numbers on torrid coasts, feeding in the shallow water pastures of sea plants near the surface.
77269-the-penny-magazine-of-the-society-:
The Penny Magazine of October 27, 1832, is number 36 of a weekly for working readers. The Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge published it every Saturday. Its lead article treats the boa constrictor at the Surrey Zoological Gardens. A woodcut shows the snake about to strike a rabbit. The boa lies curled in a large box for weeks at a time, near torpid. Snakes need food only at long intervals, the article explains.

In confinement the boa takes a whole rabbit or fowl every month or six weeks. The artist watched the snake rise and strike at a rabbit in its box. At the last inch the boa drew back, its appetite not yet keen. The rabbit then played about the scaly folds, unaware. The keeper warned that the respite would be brief. Cheap print carried natural history to a mass audience.
britannica-1911-chi-fu:
Chi-fu, also called Chefoo or Yen-t'ai, is a seaport of northern China on the south coast of the Gulf of Chih-li, in Shan-tung province. It stands near the mouth of the Yi-ho, about 30 miles east of Têng-chow-fu. Once an unwalled village, it became that city's port and opened to foreign trade in 1858 under the treaty of Tientsin. A British consulate, a Chinese custom house and a foreign settlement grew up there.

Trade grew steadily, with imports and exports rising from £2,724,000 in 1880 to £4,909,908 in 1904, the entry reports. Ships entering rose from 905 in 1895 to 1,842 in 1905, though large vessels must moor far from shore. Imports are woollen and cotton goods, iron and opium, and exports include bean cake, raw silk and straw braid. European fleets use the anchorage, and the Chi-fu convention was signed here in 1876.
britannica-1911-corfu:
Corfu is an island of Greece in the Ionian Sea, off the coast of Albania or Epirus. A strait of two to fifteen miles splits it from that coast. Its Greek name is Kerkyra or Korkyra, and its Latin name Corcyra. The name Corfu is an Italian twist of a Byzantine word drawn from a Greek term for crests. In shape the island is not unlike a sickle.

The hollow side of the sickle, with the town and harbour of Corfu at its centre, faces the Albanian coast. The island is about forty miles long and twenty miles wide at most. Its area is put at 227 square miles, and its people numbered 99,571 in 1907. Two high ranges split it into three districts. The north is hilly, the centre rolls, and the south lies low.
britannica-1911-kiu-kiang-fu:
Kiu-kiang Fu is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a prefectural city in the Chinese province of Kiang-si. The city stands on the south bank of the Yangtsze, fifteen miles above the point where the Kan river flows in from the Po-yang lake. Its north face is parted from the river by only a road's width. Its walls run five to six miles round and are stronger and broader than usual.

The article traces the city's many names and hard history. Under the Tsin dynasty it was Sin-Yang, and it took its present name under the Ming. It has been besieged many times and was last taken in February 1853, when the T'ai-p'ing rebels looted and destroyed it so fully that only one street remained. The article then explains its trade value: the river, the lake channels and the tea districts.
britannica-1911-kyosai-sho-fu:
Sho-fu Kyosai (1831–1889) was a Japanese painter, born at Koga in the province of Shimotsuke in 1831. As a boy he worked for a time with Kuniyoshi, then trained in the studio of Kano Dohaku. He soon left his master's formal ways for the freer popular school. In the turmoil that brought the revolution of 1867 he won a name as a caricaturist. The shogunate's officers arrested and jailed him three times for his work.

After the mikado took power, a great congress of painters and men of letters was held, and Kyosai spoke his mind again in a caricature. It pleased the crowd and brought him to the police once more, this time of the other party. He is held the greatest heir of Hokusai, though not his pupil, and the first political caricaturist of Japan. His art is wild and free, with draughtsmanship of very great skill.
britannica-1911-si-gan-fu:
Si-gan Fu is the subject of a city entry in the 1911 Britannica. The city was the chief town of Shen-si in north west China. Its state name was given as Sian Fu. A first emperor set his chief city on its site. That reign ran in the years before Christ. Name forms changed as houses rose and fell. In Tang, Sung, Yuan, and Ming times it bore new names.

For long spans the city was the seat of the empire. In size, souls, and wealth it still ranked high. In 1900 the court fled there when Peking fell. For a year it served as the seat of rule once more. The city forms a square ringed by strong walls. Its gates are praised as finer than those of Peking. Its count was said to be one million souls. A great road to Central Asia runs past its walls.
britannica-1911-wen-chow-fu:
Wên-chow-fu, a city in China, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is a prefectural city in the province of Cheh-kiang. It was one of five ports opened to foreign trade by the Chifu convention. It stands on the south bank of the river Gow, about twenty miles from the sea. Its people were put at eighty thousand.

The site, the text says, was chosen by Kwo P'oh, a famed antiquary of old China. He saw in the peaks nearby a pattern like the stars of the Great Bear. From that, the town was first known as the Great Bear city. Later, a white deer was seen nearby with a flower in its mouth. That was taken as a lucky omen. It more than justified a change of name to Luh, or Deer city. Town lore here is woven into the map itself.
britannica-1911-yang-chow-fu:
The 1911 Britannica article on Yang-chow Fu describes a prefectural city in Kiangsu, China. It forms two distinct cities on the Grand Canal. Its population was about 100,000. Its walls run between three and four miles around. The streets are well supplied with shops. The city has fine temples and colleges.

The account notes the city's ties with outsiders. A serious religious outbreak struck in 1868. That year Hudson Taylor opened a mission station there. The city is now a centre of Protestant missions in the province. Its link with foreigners is much older. Marco Polo ruled over it for three years. He held the post by appointment from Kublai Khan. The years were about 1282 to 1285.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corfu:
Sophrone Pétridès's entry covers the Archdiocese of Corfu, one of the Ionian Islands at the Adriatic's entrance, opposite the Albanian coast across a narrow channel. Its modern name corrupts Korphoi, the Byzantine Greek name for the chief town, pronounced Corfu. The ancient name for island and city was Cercyra or Corcyra, identified with Homeric Scheria, where Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, hosted Ulysses, and Nausicaa's father reigned.

In 735 B.C. Corinthian colonists under Chersicrates settled the island. Its navy and trade grew until, as early as 664 B.C., it could wage war on Corinth. During the Peloponnesian War, allied with Athens, Corfu fitted out 120 ships and overcame its suzerain. Internal strife soon decayed its power, while the people sided with Athens. The island enjoys a mild, salubrious climate.
doe-osti-3000609-ground-truth-for-csp-mi:
Randolph Brost, Nicholas Phelps, Zoe Wilf and co-workers at Sandia National Laboratories build ground truth for mirror measurement in report SAND2025-13532, printed October 2025. Concentrating solar power plants aim thousands of mirrors at one tower, and each mirror's shape must be measured honestly. Optical test methods grade mirrors by the light patterns they return, but a method cannot be trusted until checked against something known perfectly.

Two families of methods are examined: reflective 2f tests, which read a colour target bounced in the mirror, and gravity-directed laser methods. Against them stand two physical standards, a still water pool, nature's flattest mirror, and a high-precision reference mirror. The team tuned distances between mirror, target and camera to widen the low-error zone. A cheaper mirror's flaws showed at once in the same test, proving the method separates good glass from bad. Mirror makers get a yardstick with known marks.
doe-osti-3003145-uncertainty-quantificat:
Brian J. Williams, Troy Michael Holland, and Matthew Ryan Phillips of Los Alamos give a methods roadmap in report LA-UR-25-31138, issued November 12, 2025. The problem is uncertainty quantification for smooth functional data: experiments whose output is a whole curve, such as strain versus stress, rather than a single number. Material property studies produce curves like these by the hundreds.

The recipe runs in steps. Curves are first registered onto a common set of index values. Principal component analysis then compresses them, keeping the few modes that explain at least a user-set share of variance, typically 99 percent. Regression on each mode's scores ties curves to experiment settings. Sampling from the fitted model yields predicted mean and bounding curves at new settings. An example uses stress and strain measured on a foam core punch.
doe-osti-3017995-heavy-duty-hydrogen-ref:
Sam Sprik of the National Laboratory of the Rockies was technical contact, with Ethan Hecht and Amgad Elgowainy also named on the record, for this February 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5700-98064. The subject is heavy-duty hydrogen fueling: stations built to serve class 8 long-haul trucks, which need large amounts of hydrogen delivered fast.

The work had four parts. First, a reference station design. Second, design concepts for a fueling performance test device. Third, a station capacity model. Fourth, near-real-time fuel quality verification using on-site hydrogen contaminant detectors, for both light-duty and heavy-duty stations. Staff and equipment came from three national laboratories, Sandia, the Rockies laboratory, and Argonne, with industry cost share. Sizing tables work through tube diameters for gaseous hydrogen stations under the HYRAM+ risk model. Truck fleet planners get the engineering scaffolding for stations that do not yet exist at scale.
manchu-the-trail-of-fu:
The Trail of Fu Manchu is a thriller by Sax Rohmer. It opens in the great London fog of 1934, the worst in memory. Constable Ireland raises his red lantern and challenges a sound in the mist. Something breathes hard and creeps past him, unseen and unanswering.

Traffic stands still, and king fog holds the city in bondage. Such is the doorway into Fu Manchu's latest plot against the West. Rohmer's Chinese mastermind works through secret agents and strange science. Nayland Smith and his allies race to break the trail. The tale is pure pulp menace, thick with fog and dread. It shows the Fu Manchu series at full stretch.
nasa-tm-19670006721-secondary-flow-rates:
J. Z. Adamson, of the Test Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, wrote this memorandum on December 1, 1966. Numbered TM X-53543, it measures secondary flow rates in a vertical diffuser, a widening duct that slows a fast stream. A rocket exhaust jet serves as the motive fluid, pulling a secondary water flow along with it.

Adamson shortened the diffuser step by step and recorded how the secondary flow responded at each length. Figures in the report show the original diffuser layout and a flame deflector scale model of the Saturn V test facility. Other figures chart the major and minor effects of reduced length, plus typical diffuser pressures. Tables collect the engine and diffuser parameters and summarize the test data behind the results and conclusions.
ruth-fielding-in-moving-pictures-or-help: Alice B. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding in Moving Pictures, or Helping the Dormitory Fund, issued in New York by Cupples and Leon. Emerson is named as author of Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill, Ruth Fielding on Cliff Island, and other books in the same series. A series list for girls follows the title page, giving the Ruth Fielding books in order.
the-outdoor-girls-of-deepdale-or-camping: Laura Lee Hope published The Outdoor Girls of Deepdale in 1913. The subtitle promises camping and tramping for fun and health, and the book is the first of the series. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents list chapters from A Fluttering Paper and The Tramping Club onward. Amy's Mystery, The Leaky Boat, The Missing Lunch, and The Deserted House follow. The list shows the shape of the girls' first camping tour.
